name: Group polarisation
statement: Discussion among people who already lean the same way moves their average position further in that direction, which is why the original 'risky shift' label was abandoned.
meaning: The claim is about an average, and about a direction. Members of a group state a position privately, talk, and state it again. Myers and Lamm's group polarisation hypothesis is that the average of the second set of responses will be more extreme than the average of the first, in the same direction the first set already leaned. Two things it does not mean. It is not a claim that the group splits into opposed camps, which is the ordinary sense of the word and which Myers and Lamm flag as different from the technical one. It is not a claim about individuals either. Fraser, Gouge and Billig's example, as Myers and Lamm report it, has three people at +3, +1 and -2 on a seven-point scale all settling on +1 after discussion. The mean moves from +0.67 to +1, so the group has polarised, and no member is more extreme than before. Since group members generally converge, Myers and Lamm call that pattern typical. The related idea of extremisation, movement away from neutrality in any direction, is broader: every polarisation is an extremisation, and not the reverse.

origin.where: an M.S. thesis at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, School of Industrial Management, supervised by Donald G. Marquis
origin.note: The thesis is 'A comparison of individual and group decisions involving risk', read here in full from MIT's repository. Stoner set out to test the belief that groups are more cautious than individuals, and found the reverse. One hundred and one graduate students answered twelve choice-dilemmas problems alone, seventy-eight of them then met a week later in thirteen six-man groups and worked to a unanimous decision on each problem, and twenty-three served as controls. Twelve of the thirteen groups shifted risky on more questions than they shifted cautious, which a two-tailed sign test put at p = .0005. One problem, question 12, moved the other way, and that single item is what later work on cautious shifts was built on. The name came later and from other people. Myers and Lamm credit the term to Moscovici and his colleagues, whose 1969 paper is titled 'The group as a polarizer of attitudes', and their own 1976 review turned it into a general hypothesis.

evidence: The choice-dilemmas task asks for the lowest probability of success at which a character should attempt a risky option, on a scale from 1 in 10 to 10 in 10. Myers and Lamm report that groups came out riskier than the average of their members, generally by about one scale unit or less, and that the result was found in a dozen different nations. They also report that group decision making is not needed for it: a short discussion followed by private answers shifts the average too. Then the direction reversed on some items. Stoner's study of widely held values, read here as the MIT working paper of October 1967 rather than as the 1968 journal article, sorted life-situation items by the values his participants held and by how risky they rated themselves against other people like them. It ran 212 subjects, of whom 190 met in 33 groups of four to seven members. On all six items whose widely held values favoured risk, the unanimous group decisions came out riskier than the members' individual average, and the gap reached significance on every one. Four of the five items classified as caution-oriented shifted cautious, and only two of those four shifts reached significance. Myers and Lamm treat the reversal as settled and call the risky-shift label a misnomer. What replaced it was an item-level regularity. Across items, the mean initial response and the mean shift correlate at generally .70 to .90, a figure Myers and Lamm attribute to Teger and Pruitt. Stoner's own twelve items give r = -.89, negative because a lower probability stands for a riskier choice. Items starting below about 6 in 10 tend to shift risky, and items starting above 7 in 10 often shift the other way. Myers and Lamm add two cautions of their own. The same correlation taken across groups within a single item is near zero, and fixing a neutral point by post hoc regression and then testing the hypothesis against it is circular. Moscovici and Zavalloni had already found the same shape outside risk, with French students' positive view of De Gaulle and negative view of Americans both strengthening after discussion, as Myers and Lamm describe it. Two mechanisms carried the later literature: comparison with the positions of others, and the pool of arguments a discussion brings out.

examples.tag: The residents' meeting about a new road
examples.text: Everyone arrives already mildly against the scheme. After an hour the average opposition is stronger, and the one member who came strongly against it has softened towards the rest. The mean has moved without anyone dividing.

examples.tag: A book group that liked the novel
examples.text: Members rate the book warmly before the discussion and more warmly after it. Nobody has split off into a rival camp. The shift is in where the average sits, which is the only thing the claim is about.

examples.tag: The investment club that played safe
examples.text: A club whose members individually lean towards the cautious option settles, after talking it through, on something safer than the average member first proposed. The discussion moved the group further along the way it already leaned.

replication.headline: The original claim, that groups decide more riskily than their members, did not survive the 1960s; the restated claim about shifting toward the pre-existing lean holds in most tests, though its own reviewers call the shift small and often absent.
replication.detail: Myers and Lamm reviewed group discussion experiments on attitudes, jury decisions, ethical decisions, judgments, person perception, negotiation and risk measures other than choice dilemmas, and found them generally consistent with the polarisation hypothesis. Their own summary is guarded. Group enhancement of initial mean tendencies is not always observed, they write, and when it does occur it is generally of small absolute magnitude. They add that negative results have probably gone unreported more often than rejections of the null, citing Greenwald. The clearest test outside the laboratory is Schkade, Sunstein and Hastie's Colorado study. Sixty-three citizens were recruited in Boulder, a liberal city, and Colorado Springs, a conservative one, and put in ten like-minded groups. They discussed global warming, affirmative action and civil unions, rating each issue privately on a one-to-ten scale before and after fifteen minutes of discussion. Twenty-six of the thirty group discussions, 87 per cent, moved the individual mean in the direction the group already leaned. The difference in shift between the two locations gave F(1,61) = 56.1, p < .001. The gap between the two towns' means widened from 4.59 before discussion to 6.24 after, p < .001. Laboratory work continues to produce the effect and to argue about its cause. Sieber and Ziegler manipulated cognitive load while presenting a group's average attitude and a set of arguments about a tunnel project. They collected data from 152 students and analysed 147. With capacity restrained, a high group average produced more polarisation than a low one, M = 3.51 against M = 0.06, F(1, 139) = 3.96, p < .05, d = 0.43, with an interval of 0.04 to 0.81 whose level the paper does not state. With capacity unrestrained, that difference vanished and argument strength did the work instead.

study.cite: Schkade, D., Sunstein, C. R., & Hastie, R. (2007). What happened on Deliberation Day? California Law Review, 95(3), 915-940.

limits: No effect size for the polarisation effect itself is quoted here, because none was obtained from a paper that was opened. Isenberg's 1986 meta-analysis is closed at the publisher, and its abstract survives at OpenAlex only as an opening fragment that breaks off in mid-sentence, giving the span it reviewed as 1974 to 1982. Crossref deposits no abstract for it, Semantic Scholar records the field as withheld by the publisher, and the APA record page answers a bot challenge. A previous version of this page said no abstract could be had, which was true of the two indexes it named and wrong of the third. Isenberg's mean effect sizes of r = .44 for mere exposure and r = .75 for persuasive arguments are quoted here from Sieber and Ziegler's description of them, not from Isenberg, and they are for the two proposed mechanisms rather than for polarisation as such. They sit outside the structured fields for that reason, as does Sieber and Ziegler's own interval, because that paper never says what level it carries. Stoner's 1961 thesis was read in full from MIT's repository, which corrects a previous note here saying its text was not served without authentication. The 1968 journal article was not opened, because Elsevier answers with a bot challenge, so the figures above come from the MIT working paper of October 1967, numbered 289-67, which carries the same title and is what the open-access indexes point at. The two versions were not compared. That working paper also disagrees with itself about which item its two classification methods sorted differently, naming item 6 in one paragraph and item 5 in the next. Moscovici and Zavalloni's paper, Fraser, Gouge and Billig's paper and Cartwright's 1971 assessment of the choice-dilemmas literature were verified as bibliographic records only, with no abstract deposited at Crossref or OpenAlex, and what they contain is reported here through Myers and Lamm. Iyengar and colleagues' review is indexed as open access, and its publisher answers a bot challenge rather than a paywall, so only its abstract was read. A search of Crossref, PubMed, record lookups at OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar, and general web search on 21 September 2026 found no meta-analysis of group polarisation after Isenberg's, and no multi-site replication of a choice-dilemmas or group-discussion polarisation experiment. The search endpoints at OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar refused queries that day on budget and rate limits, so neither index was searched. The nearest preregistered work the search did turn up is Daneshi and Brass, who had 99 online participants inflate virtual balloons beside computer-generated agents and saw risk taking rise as more agents inflated riskily, which is not a group discussion. Nyhan and colleagues report 23,377 valid survey completions from 28,296 eligible participants, and the figure used here is the analysed one. Boxell and colleagues' article carries a 2018 correction for a reversed sex coding, which its authors say changes no statement in the paper. The Colorado study is one country, three issues and ten groups, and its participants were recruited to be like-minded, which is the condition the effect needs.
misreadings: Groupthink is the commonest confusion, and it is a different claim, set out at entry no. 36. Turner and Pratkanis state Janis's chain: antecedent conditions foster the extreme consensus seeking that gives the model its name, which produces symptoms such as illusion of invulnerability and stereotypes of outgroups, which produce defective decision making. That is a claim about decision quality. Group polarisation is a claim about the direction an average moves, and it says nothing about whether the new position is better or worse. The second confusion is the word itself. In political science, polarisation usually means a population dividing, and Iyengar and colleagues use affective polarisation for partisans coming to dislike and distrust the other party. Myers and Lamm's polarisation is an increase in the extremity of one sample's average, and a group can polarise in their sense while every member becomes less extreme. The third is treating the risky shift as the finding. It is the special case that started the field and the label its own reviewers dropped. The fourth is the online story. Bail and colleagues paid Twitter users to follow a bot retweeting the other side for a month. Republicans became more conservative rather than less, by 0.12 points on a seven-point scale as the most cautious estimate and 0.60 points among the fully compliant. The shift among Democrats was toward the liberal end and not statistically reliable. Nyhan and colleagues went the other way. They cut 23,377 Facebook users' exposure to like-minded sources by about a third for three months around the 2020 election, and found no measurable effect on eight preregistered measures, among them affective polarisation and ideological extremity. Their equivalence test rules out effects of 0.12 standard deviations or more on each. Boxell, Gentzkow and Shapiro report that American polarisation rose fastest in the demographic groups least likely to use the internet, their index and all but one of its component measures growing more among people over 65 than among people aged 18 to 39. Echo chambers are real as a description of what people see. Their effect on attitudes is not the laboratory effect scaled up.
